rule_name: Paragraph Breaks, Keep One Beat in One Paragraph
quote: We'll get you a bigger one.
why: this line and the reply that follows are set as isolated one-line paragraphs cut off from the porch beat they belong to, splitting a continuous moment into artificially separate events (this is Rule 14's own cited violation example, reproduced verbatim)
suggestion: Fold it into the same paragraph as the porch beat: "Her mother watches from the porch with a coffee. 'We'll get you a bigger one.' 'It's fine.'"

quote: the thing Chloe has not built at all
why: 'the thing' stands in for whatever Chloe does here as vague emotional shorthand instead of a specific, nameable action
suggestion: Then there is the sound Chloe has not made before, the stairs, the door.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the thing I keep asking you for
why: 'the thing' is the exact placeholder Rule 27 names for behavior that should be shown instead of labeled; what the matching actually requires is never rendered
suggestion: She's doing the breath-drop before the note that I keep asking you for

rule_name: Talking Heads, Anchor Dialogue in Physical Space
why: this opens a six-turn exchange (through line 73) with no physical detail dropped in after the initial framing, so the argument reads as a transcript rather than two bodies in a front hall
suggestion: Add a beat mid-run, e.g. her mother resettling the phone book on the hall table before "Ellie Peterson is ten years old..."

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
quote: You're not at school. Are you.
why: six consecutive dialogue turns (63-73) carry no attribution at all, so the reader has to track who is speaking purely by counting line breaks and inferring from content
suggestion: "You're not at school," her mother says. "Are you."
